notes.front: What is a "normal user" in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A human user managed outside the cluster; Kubernetes has no User object and cannot add users through the API.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes assumes a separate system, such as private keys or a user store, manages people; only their credentials are checked at request time.
notes.example: Like a building that checks ID cards issued by an outside authority, rather than keeping its own list of residents.

notes.front: What is an authentication module (authenticator)?
notes.back: A plugin the API server runs to try to identify who is making a request, from client certificates, bearer tokens, or a proxy.
notes.explanation: Several authenticators can be enabled at once; each is tried in turn until one succeeds.
notes.example: Like a security desk that checks an ID card, then a fob, then a visitor badge, one after another.

notes.front: What attributes does an authenticator attach to a request?
notes.back: Username, UID, groups, and an "extra" map of additional string data.
notes.explanation: These values are opaque to authentication; they only matter later, when an authorizer reads them.
notes.example: Like a visitor badge that lists a name, a badge number, a department, and a few notes.

notes.front: What is an anonymous request?
notes.back: A request no configured authenticator rejects, given the username system:anonymous and group system:unauthenticated.
notes.explanation: It matters because an anonymous request can still be authorized if RBAC rules grant that group access.
notes.example: Like a visitor who shows no ID at all, but is waved through because no one checks the sign-in sheet.

notes.front: What is the system:authenticated group?
notes.back: The group the API server automatically adds every successfully authenticated user to.
notes.explanation: It sits alongside any custom groups an authenticator assigns, and can itself be bound in RBAC.
notes.example: Like an automatic "verified" tag given to anyone who badges in, on top of their department tag.

notes.front: What is X.509 client certificate authentication?
notes.back: Authenticating a client by a certificate signed by the cluster's trusted CA; the certificate's common name gives the username.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes uses this for system components such as the kubelet, and it can also authenticate people.
notes.example: Like an ID badge issued and signed by the building's own security office.

notes.front: What is a bearer token?
notes.back: A token sent in an HTTP "Authorization: Bearer" header; whoever presents it is treated as its owner.
notes.explanation: Static tokens, bootstrap tokens, service account tokens, OpenID Connect and webhook authentication are all forms of bearer token.
notes.example: Like a numbered ticket that grants entry to whoever is holding it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authenticating", "Putting a bearer token in a request"

notes.front: What is a static token file?
notes.back: A CSV of tokens loaded into the API server at start-up (--token-auth-file); changing it needs a restart.
notes.explanation: The hardening guide calls it unsuitable for production: credentials sit in clear text on disk with no rotation or lockout.
notes.example: Like a paper guest list taped to the front desk that only a new print run can update.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms", "Static token file"

notes.front: What is a bootstrap token?
notes.back: A dynamically managed bearer token, stored as a Secret in kube-system, used to join new nodes to a cluster.
notes.explanation: It authenticates as system:bootstrap:<Token ID> in the deliberately limited system:bootstrappers group, so it isn't fit for ordinary user access.
notes.example: Like a one-time construction pass that opens only the site gate, not the whole building.

notes.front: What is OpenID Connect (OIDC)?
notes.back: An OAuth2-based protocol whose signed ID token the API server can accept as a bearer token; recommended for production users.
notes.explanation: Because the ID token carries everything needed to verify identity, the API server never has to contact the identity provider on each request.
notes.example: Like showing a signed, sealed pass from an outside identity office instead of a locally issued badge.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authenticating: OpenID Connect tokens" and "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms"

notes.front: What is a JSON Web Token (JWT)?
notes.back: A signed token format with well-known fields; OIDC ID tokens and Kubernetes service account tokens are both JWTs.
notes.explanation: Because the signature can be checked locally, a JWT lets the API server verify each token without asking the issuer about that token.
notes.example: Like a tamper-evident seal on an envelope: anyone can check it's intact without contacting the sender.

notes.front: What is webhook token authentication?
notes.back: The API server posts a TokenReview containing the bearer token to an external HTTP service, which replies whether it's valid.
notes.explanation: It lets Kubernetes delegate authentication decisions to systems it doesn't otherwise integrate with, such as LDAP or Kerberos gateways.
notes.example: Like phoning an outside credentials office to check a badge before letting someone in.

notes.front: What is an authenticating proxy?
notes.back: A reverse proxy in front of the API server that authenticates the caller itself and passes the username and groups in request headers.
notes.explanation: The API server trusts those headers completely, so the link between proxy and API server must be secured or an attacker could forge them.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who checks ID and tells the office "this is Alice from Sales" — the office just trusts the receptionist.

notes.front: What is user impersonation in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Acting as another user, group or service account by setting impersonation headers, when authorized to do so.
notes.explanation: It lets a trusted administrator test what another identity can do, without logging in as them.
notes.example: Like a manager using a "log in as" feature to see exactly what an employee's account can access.

notes.front: What is a service account token?
notes.back: A signed JWT that authenticates a ServiceAccount, checked for signature, expiry, audience and object binding.
notes.explanation: It is the standard identity a Pod uses to talk to the API server, distinct from a human user's credentials.
notes.example: Like a staff pass issued to a machine or a robot rather than to a person.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Authenticating service account credentials"

notes.front: What is the TokenRequest API?
notes.back: An API that issues short-lived, audience-bound tokens for a ServiceAccount, instead of a long-lived Secret.
notes.explanation: It is the mechanism behind the tokens the kubelet has automatically mounted into Pods since v1.22.
notes.example: Like a day pass printed fresh each morning instead of a permanent key that never changes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Manually retrieve ServiceAccount credentials"

notes.front: What is a bound service account token?
notes.back: A time-limited TokenRequest token, tied to an audience and an object such as a Pod; it expires when that object is deleted.
notes.explanation: Binding the token's life to the Pod's means a stolen token from a deleted Pod stops working immediately.
notes.example: Like a conference badge that is deactivated the moment its holder checks out.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Authenticating service account credentials"

notes.front: What is a projected service account token volume?
notes.back: The projected volume the kubelet uses to mount an auto-rotating bound token, the cluster CA certificate, and the Pod's namespace into a Pod.
notes.explanation: The kubelet fetches the token through the TokenRequest API and refreshes it before it expires, so the application never handles an expired credential.
notes.example: Like a hotel key card the front desk silently re-issues before it expires.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Managing Service Accounts", "Bound service account token volume mechanism"

notes.front: What is a legacy service account token Secret?
notes.back: A long-lived token in a Secret; one you create by hand never expires. Since v1.29, unused auto-generated legacy tokens are purged after a year.
notes.explanation: Because a hand-created one never expires, its exposure risk is open-ended: anyone who can read that Secret can authenticate as the account indefinitely.
notes.example: Like a permanent master key that was cut once and never gets recalled.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Manage Service Accounts", "Clean up Legacy ServiceAccount Token Secrets"

notes.front: What does automountServiceAccountToken: false do?
notes.back: Stops a ServiceAccount's token being automatically mounted into Pods, set on the ServiceAccount or overridden per Pod.
notes.explanation: Most Pods never call the Kubernetes API, so mounting a token they don't need only adds attack surface.
notes.example: Like not issuing a building pass to a role that never needs to enter the building.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Assign a ServiceAccount to a Pod"

notes.front: What is a token's audience?
notes.back: The intended recipient of a token; the service receiving the token should check that it matches itself.
notes.explanation: Checking the audience stops a token meant for one service being replayed against another.
notes.example: Like checking a ticket is for tonight's show, not just any show at the venue.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Authenticating service account credentials in your own code"

notes.front: Why should you only use kubeconfig files from trusted sources?
notes.back: A specially crafted kubeconfig file could run malicious code or expose local files when kubectl reads it.
notes.explanation: If you must use an untrusted kubeconfig file, inspect it carefully first, much as you would a shell script.
notes.example: Like being wary of a USB stick handed to you by a stranger, even though it looks like a settings file.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files"

notes.front: When multiple authenticator modules are enabled, the {{c1::first module to successfully authenticate}} the request short-circuits evaluation, and the API server does not guarantee the order they run in.
notes.explanation: This is why enabling too many authenticators makes it hard to predict which one identified a given request.

notes.front: When is anonymous access enabled by default in Kubernetes?
notes.back: Whenever the API server uses an authorization mode other than AlwaysAllow.
notes.explanation: It can be turned off with --anonymous-auth=false on the API server.

notes.front: With token authentication and anonymous access both configured, what happens if a request carries an invalid bearer token?
notes.back: A 401 Unauthorized error, not treatment as an anonymous request.
notes.explanation: Only a request with no bearer token at all is treated as anonymous; a bad token is a failed authentication.

notes.front: With X.509 client certificate authentication, Kubernetes takes the username from the {{c1::commonName field}} of the certificate's subject, and group memberships from its organization (O) fields.
notes.explanation: A certificate with several O fields places its holder in several groups at once.

notes.front: Can a Kubernetes client certificate be revoked once issued?
notes.back: No. Kubernetes does not support certificate revocation; any issued certificate stays valid until it expires.
notes.explanation: This is why the hardening guide recommends short lifetimes for certificates used to authenticate people.

notes.front: What username and group does a node's client certificate give the kubelet?
notes.back: Username system:node:<node name>, in the system:nodes group.
notes.explanation: This identity is what the Node authorization mode checks against when deciding what a kubelet can do.

notes.front: A bootstrap token has the form {{c1::[a-z0-9]{6}.[a-z0-9]{16}}}, a Token ID followed by a Token Secret.
notes.explanation: The API server must be started with --enable-bootstrap-token-auth for this authenticator to be active.

notes.front: What claims must a minimal valid JWT payload contain to authenticate to Kubernetes?
notes.back: iss (issuer), aud (audience), exp (expiry), and the configured username claim.
notes.explanation: The API server checks the signature and these claims before treating the token as a valid identity.

notes.front: Which OAuth2 token does kubectl send as the bearer token in OIDC authentication?
notes.back: The id_token, not the access_token.
notes.explanation: The id_token is the signed JWT that carries the user's identity claims for the API server to verify.

notes.front: What is the default cache time-to-live for a webhook authentication decision?
notes.back: Two minutes, set by --authentication-token-webhook-cache-ttl.
notes.explanation: Caching avoids calling the external service on every single request that reuses the same token.

notes.front: What username and groups does a ServiceAccount authenticate with?
notes.back: Username system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:<name>, in groups system:serviceaccounts and system:serviceaccounts:<namespace>.
notes.explanation: These are the exact strings an RBAC RoleBinding needs to target that ServiceAccount.

notes.front: What is the default lifespan of a token issued by the TokenRequest API, and who refreshes it?
notes.back: One hour by default; the kubelet refreshes the mounted token before it expires.
notes.explanation: The short default lifespan limits how long a leaked token stays useful.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Managing Service Accounts", "Bound service account token volume mechanism"

notes.front: How is a bound service account token invalidated before its normal expiry?
notes.back: By deleting the Pod it is bound to; there is no other mechanism to invalidate a TokenRequest token.
notes.explanation: This makes deleting the Pod the way to immediately cut off a token you no longer trust.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Managing Service Accounts", "Bound service account token volume mechanism"

notes.front: What is the recommended minimum set of authentication methods for a cluster?
notes.back: Service account tokens for ServiceAccounts, plus at least one other method for normal user authentication.
notes.explanation: One authenticator alone can't cover both machine and human identities, which have different needs.

notes.front: For production clusters with multiple users accessing the API directly, what authentication source does the hardening guide recommend?
notes.back: An external source such as OIDC; internal mechanisms like client certificates and service account tokens are not suitable.
notes.explanation: Internal mechanisms lack revocation and rotation, which becomes a bigger problem the more people share a cluster.

notes.front: Why is write access to Secrets dangerous when service account tokens can be stored in them?
notes.back: Anyone with write access to Secrets can request a token, and anyone with read access can authenticate as that ServiceAccount.
notes.explanation: This is why RBAC good practice restricts both write and read access to Secrets tightly.

notes.front: Why does Kubernetes recommend the TokenReview API over OIDC discovery for validating service account tokens in your own code?
notes.back: TokenReview invalidates tokens bound to deleted objects immediately; OIDC validation treats the token as valid until it expires.
notes.explanation: If a Pod is deleted, an application checking with TokenReview will reject its token right away; one relying on OIDC discovery won't.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Authenticating service account credentials in your own code"

notes.front: Can a user's group membership be changed while their client certificate is still valid?
notes.back: No. Group data is embedded in the certificate's organization fields and is fixed for the certificate's lifetime.
notes.explanation: Changing someone's groups means issuing them a new certificate, since the old one keeps its original claims.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms", "X.509 client certificate authentication"

notes.front: A cluster uses RBAC (not AlwaysAllow) and anonymous access hasn't been disabled. A request arrives with no Authorization header at all. What identity does it get?
notes.back: system:anonymous, in group system:unauthenticated.
notes.explanation: Anonymous access is on by default unless the cluster is set to allow every request automatically, and a missing token (not an invalid one) is what triggers it.

notes.front: An external CI system outside the cluster needs a Kubernetes credential for a long-running job. What should it use rather than a legacy token Secret?
notes.back: A short-lived TokenRequest token, refreshed as needed, rather than a non-expiring Secret token.
notes.explanation: The Kubernetes project recommends against long-lived bearer tokens because, once disclosed, they can be misused indefinitely.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Manually retrieve ServiceAccount credentials"

notes.front: A Pod only renders images and never calls the Kubernetes API. What setting removes an unnecessary credential from it?
notes.back: automountServiceAccountToken: false, on the Pod or its ServiceAccount.
notes.explanation: A token the Pod never uses is still a credential an attacker inside the container could steal.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Assign a ServiceAccount to a Pod"

notes.front: An administrator wants to give a new employee daily kubectl access using a bootstrap token. Is that appropriate?
notes.back: No. Bootstrap tokens have hard-coded, narrow group memberships meant only for joining nodes, not for user access.
notes.explanation: Using them for people also inherits their lack of a lockout mechanism against guessing.

notes.front: A team wants to add a new user by editing a static token file and restarting the API server each time. Is this suitable for a production cluster?
notes.back: No. Credentials sit in clear text on control-plane disks, and every change needs a restart, with no lockout mechanism.
notes.explanation: This is exactly why the hardening guide lists the static token file as unsuitable for production.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms", "Static token file"

notes.front: An administrator wants to check exactly what a low-privileged user can do, without logging in as them. What lets them do this?
notes.back: User impersonation, using an impersonation header, if the administrator is authorized to impersonate that user.
notes.explanation: kubectl auth can-i --as <user> uses this mechanism to run the check as that identity.

notes.front: A colleague emails you a kubeconfig file "to save time setting up your cluster access". Should you load it straight into kubectl?
notes.back: No. Only use kubeconfig files from trusted sources; a crafted one can run malicious code or expose files.
notes.explanation: Treat an unfamiliar kubeconfig file with the same caution as an unfamiliar shell script.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files"

notes.front: A company already runs its own LDAP-backed credential service and wants Kubernetes to check bearer tokens against it directly. Which authenticator fits?
notes.back: Webhook token authentication, which posts the token to that external service for a decision.
notes.explanation: It lets Kubernetes integrate with authentication systems it doesn't natively speak, without building a new authenticator.

notes.front: A service accepts any bearer token that passes signature checks, without looking at its audience. What risk does this create?
notes.back: A token issued for a different service could be replayed against this one.
notes.explanation: Checking the audience keeps a token scoped to the application it was meant for.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Authenticating service account credentials in your own code"

notes.front: What is the difference between an invalid bearer token and no bearer token at all?
notes.back: An invalid token gets a 401 Unauthorized error; no token at all is treated as an anonymous request.
notes.explanation: Both fail to authenticate as a real user, but only the second is eligible for anonymous access rules.
notes.contrast: One is a rejected attempt at proof; the other is simply no attempt.

notes.front: What is the difference between OIDC and webhook token authentication?
notes.back: OIDC checks the token's signature and claims itself; webhook authentication asks an external service to decide, caching each answer briefly.
notes.explanation: OIDC scales better because it avoids a round trip per request; webhook decisions are cached, by default for two minutes, rather than looked up fresh each time.
notes.contrast: One checks a signature; the other asks someone else to decide.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authenticating", "OpenID Connect tokens" and "Webhook token authentication"

notes.front: What is the difference between a bound service account token and a legacy service account token Secret?
notes.back: A bound token is short-lived, audience-scoped and expires when its Pod is deleted; a legacy Secret token never expires.
notes.explanation: The bound token is the recommended mechanism since it limits how long a leaked credential stays useful.
notes.contrast: One is disposable by design; the other has to be manually revoked.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Managing Service Accounts", "Bound service account token volume mechanism" and "Manual Secret management for ServiceAccounts"

notes.front: What are the two categories of users every Kubernetes cluster has?
notes.back: ServiceAccounts, managed by Kubernetes itself, and normal users, managed by a system outside the cluster.
notes.explanation: Only ServiceAccounts exist as API objects; a normal user's identity is opaque to the API server.

notes.front: What ServiceAccount does every namespace get automatically, and what permissions does it start with?
notes.back: A "default" ServiceAccount, with no permissions beyond the default API discovery permissions RBAC grants every authenticated principal.
notes.explanation: Deleting the default ServiceAccount doesn't remove it for long: the control plane recreates it.

notes.front: By default, does Kubernetes inject ServiceAccount credentials into a Pod, or does a Pod have to opt in?
notes.back: It injects them by default, for the default ServiceAccount or any custom one specified, unless automountServiceAccountToken is set to false.
notes.explanation: This is why forgetting to set automountServiceAccountToken: false leaves a credential mounted even in Pods that never call the API.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Assign a ServiceAccount to a Pod"

notes.front: Where does kubectl look for a kubeconfig file by default?
notes.back: A file named config in $HOME/.kube, unless overridden by the KUBECONFIG environment variable or the --kubeconfig flag.
notes.explanation: "kubeconfig" describes the format, not a required filename, which is why this default matters.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Organizing Cluster Access Using kubeconfig Files"

notes.front: What header does an authenticating proxy typically use to tell the API server the caller's username?
notes.back: Whatever `--requestheader-username-headers` names; the docs' example uses X-Remote-User, and suggest X-Remote-Group for groups.
notes.explanation: The API server trusts these header values completely once request-header authentication is configured.

notes.front: What must an authenticating proxy present before the API server will trust its identity headers?
notes.back: A valid client certificate, checked against a specified CA, to prevent an attacker from spoofing those headers.
notes.explanation: Without this check, anyone able to reach the API server directly could forge the identity headers themselves.

notes.front: Which TokenReview API version does the API server send to a webhook authenticator by default?
notes.back: authentication.k8s.io/v1beta1, for backwards compatibility; v1 requires --authentication-token-webhook-version=v1.
notes.explanation: A webhook implementer must check the apiVersion field and reply using that same version.

notes.front: A static token file is a CSV with at least {{c1::token, user name, user uid, and an optional comma-separated group list}} per line.
notes.explanation: Multiple groups must be double-quoted, as in token,user,uid,"group1,group2,group3".

notes.front: If --oidc-username-prefix isn't set and the username claim isn't email, what prefix does Kubernetes add to the OIDC username?
notes.back: The issuer URL followed by #, to prevent naming clashes between identity providers.
notes.explanation: Setting the prefix to "-" disables prefixing entirely, which risks collisions with other authenticators.

notes.front: How does Kubernetes integrate with authentication protocols it has no native support for, such as LDAP, SAML or Kerberos?
notes.back: Through an authenticating proxy or an authentication webhook; of the external protocols, Kubernetes supports only JWT and OIDC natively.
notes.explanation: This is why organisations with existing identity infrastructure usually reach for one of these two extension points.

notes.front: What happened to the LegacyServiceAccountTokenNoAutoGeneration feature gate that once stopped legacy SA token creation?
notes.back: It was enabled by default from v1.24 to v1.26, then removed in v1.27 once it reached GA status, so the block became permanent.
notes.explanation: Indefinite tokens can still be created manually, but they're no longer generated automatically for every ServiceAccount.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Service Accounts", "Manually retrieve ServiceAccount credentials"

notes.front: Why should an OIDC id_token be short-lived?
notes.back: Because it can't be revoked, much like a certificate, so a short lifetime limits how long a leaked one stays valid.
notes.explanation: kubectl's OIDC authenticator handles this by refreshing the id_token using the refresh_token once it expires.

notes.front: What is the key trust difference between user impersonation and an authenticating proxy?
notes.back: With impersonation, one user asks to be treated as another; with a proxy, the API server simply trusts its claim about who made the request.
notes.explanation: This is why an authenticating proxy needs a client certificate check, while impersonation is controlled by authorization of the impersonate verb.

notes.front: A user's OIDC id_token expires every few minutes during a long kubectl session. What keeps their session working without re-authenticating each time?
notes.back: kubectl's OIDC authenticator automatically fetches a new id_token using the stored refresh_token.
notes.explanation: This is the practical answer to why short-lived id_tokens don't mean constant manual logins.

notes.front: A team configures an authenticating proxy in front of the API server but skips TLS and client-certificate checks between them, for simplicity. Is this safe?
notes.back: No. Without those checks an attacker could intercept or forge the identity headers the API server blindly trusts.
notes.explanation: The hardening guide requires securely configured TLS between proxy and API server, and the docs require a client certificate so headers cannot be spoofed.

notes.front: A short-lived integration test environment wants a fixed, never-rotated credential that's simple to set up. Is a static token file a reasonable fit there, even though it's unsuitable for production?
notes.back: Yes: the docs say it suits long-lived, static tokens that may never be rotated.
notes.explanation: Its production drawbacks (clear text on disk, restart to change, no lockout) matter far less in a disposable test environment.

notes.front: An administrator writes a static token file line as token,alice,1001,team-a,team-b, meaning to put alice in two groups. Will this parse as intended?
notes.back: No. A multi-group column must be double-quoted, e.g. token,alice,1001,"team-a,team-b", or it will be read as extra columns.
notes.explanation: This formatting detail is exactly the kind of trap that makes the static token file error-prone to hand-edit.

notes.front: An administrator tries to run kubectl create user alice to add a new normal user. Does this API object exist?
notes.back: No. Kubernetes has no User object; normal users are never added through the API, only recognised by their credentials.
notes.explanation: A person becomes a "user" simply by presenting credentials an authenticator accepts, such as a signed client certificate.

notes.front: A webhook authenticator implementation only replies with authentication.k8s.io/v1 TokenReview objects, but the API server wasn't configured for that version. What happens?
notes.back: The exchange fails, because the API server defaults to sending v1beta1 unless started with --authentication-token-webhook-version=v1.
notes.explanation: A webhook must respond using the same version it received, so a mismatch here is a configuration bug, not a policy decision.

notes.front: A new namespace is created and a Job is deployed without specifying serviceAccountName. Which ServiceAccount does it run as?
notes.back: The namespace's default ServiceAccount, automatically created with it.
notes.explanation: That default account starts with only the baseline API discovery permissions, unless someone binds it further RBAC rights.

notes.front: What is the difference between user impersonation and an authenticating proxy?
notes.back: Impersonation is one authorized user deliberately acting as another; a proxy is a trusted intermediary the API server relies on for every caller's identity.
notes.explanation: Impersonation needs the impersonate verb per request; a proxy's trust is set up once, in its client certificate configuration.
notes.contrast: Impersonation is a one-off, authorized substitution; a proxy is a standing, structural trust relationship.

notes.front: What are the three ways the docs give for a cluster-independent service to manage normal users?
notes.back: An administrator distributing private keys, a user store such as Keystone or Google Accounts, or a file of usernames and passwords.
notes.explanation: None of these run inside Kubernetes; they're examples of the outside system authentication assumes exists.

notes.front: Why must a user log in to their identity provider separately, rather than through Kubernetes itself, when using OIDC?
notes.back: Kubernetes has no web interface to trigger the authentication process or collect credentials.
notes.explanation: This is why OIDC users authenticate to the provider first, then feed the resulting id_token to kubectl.

notes.front: Can a service account bearer token be used from outside the cluster?
notes.back: Yes. Service account tokens are valid outside the cluster too, and can identify long-standing jobs that talk to the Kubernetes API.
notes.explanation: This is why a CI system without its own Kubernetes identity often authenticates using a service account token rather than a human credential.

notes.front: A short-term contractor needs cluster access that should end soon after their contract does. Should the cluster issue them a client certificate, or use OIDC against the company's identity provider?
notes.back: OIDC: disabling the account stops new tokens being issued, and short-lived id_tokens expire within minutes; a client certificate stays valid until it expires.
notes.explanation: This is exactly the production-user scenario the hardening guide has in mind when it steers away from client certificates.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms", "X.509 client certificate authentication"

notes.front: What is the difference between a static token file entry and a bootstrap token?
notes.back: A static token file entry is a hand-written, indefinitely valid CSV line; a bootstrap token is dynamically generated, meant only for joining nodes.
notes.explanation: Both are bearer tokens, but they serve very different purposes and have very different lifecycles.
notes.contrast: One is a hand-maintained list; the other is a short-purpose, dynamically managed credential.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authenticating", "Static token file" and "Bootstrap tokens"

notes.front: A presented JWT has a valid signature, but is missing the exp claim. Does the API server accept it?
notes.back: No. A minimal valid JWT payload must include iss, aud, exp and the configured username claim; a missing one fails authentication.
notes.explanation: The exp claim is what lets Kubernetes reject an otherwise well-signed token once it's meant to have expired.

notes.front: A cluster enables only client certificates as its authenticator, used by kubelets, controllers and every human administrator alike. What has this setup overlooked?
notes.back: Using one authenticator for every identity; the recommended minimum is service account tokens plus at least one separate method for people.
notes.explanation: Machine and human identities have different needs, such as revocation, that one authenticator alone rarely covers well.

notes.front: An administrator's X.509 client certificate, issued with a five-year lifetime, is stolen. What can the cluster do about it?
notes.back: Very little: the certificate cannot be revoked, only outlived, short of re-keying the CA.
notes.explanation: This is exactly why the Hardening Guide recommends short lifetimes for certificates used for user authentication.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Hardening Guide: Authentication Mechanisms", "X.509 client certificate authentication"

notes.front: A Pod's bound service account token is due to expire in 40 minutes, but the Pod is deleted 5 minutes from now. When does the token stop working?
notes.back: In 5 minutes, at Pod deletion: a bound token is invalidated the moment its Pod is deleted, ahead of its normal expiry.
notes.explanation: Deleting the Pod is the only way to invalidate a bound token early; there is no separate revocation call.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Managing Service Accounts", "Bound service account token volume mechanism"
